newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: Portugal 10-yr bond spread with Bund too wide-IGCP.
newsitem.headline: Portugal 10-yr bond spread with Bund too wide-IGCP.

text.p: The spread between Portugal's benchmark 10-year bonds and that of Germany is too wide bearing in mind that Portugal is well-placed to qualify for economic and monetary union (EMU), the state's debt manager said.

Vitor Bento, chairman of the Institute for Public Credit Management (IGCP) told Reuters in an interview that the recent widening of the spread was due to "unfortunate and inopportune remarks by some European officials."
The spread between the Portuguese benchmark February 2007 bond and its Bund equivalent stands at over 120 basis points against less than 85 a month ago.
"The current spread (of the February 2007 against Germany) is too much taking into account that, until very recently, it was much lower," he said.

Statements by some northern European business and political leaders urging Portugal and other southern European members of the European Union to wait before seeking to join monetary union have helped undermine confidence that these countries will join in the first wave in 1999.
"As confidence is restored that Portugal is in condition to join monetary union, the spread will narrow again," he said.
But he declined to be drawn on how wide it should be.
However, Bento said that the shorter end of the yield curve, where the spread was widest, clearly had the greatest potential for narrowing the gap with Germany as monetary union approached.
The spread between Portuguese two-year issues and the bund equivalent stands at over 230 basis points.
"It is natural that in the two years that separate us from monetary union that the narrowing of the spread at the shorter end is bigger than at the longer end," he said.

The fact that yields at the longer end were lower in Portugal than in Spain while the reverse was true at the shorter end was due to central bank money market rates being higher in the former, he said.
The Bank of Portugal's repo rate stands at 6.50 percent against 6.0 percent in Spain and three percent in Germany.
But he refused to comment on whether there was space for the Bank of Portugal to cut rates further.
Bento said that lumping Portugal, Spain and Italy together in a so-called 'Club Med' made neither geographic nor economic sense.

He said it would be just as reasonable to create a 'PIAF' -- Portugal, Ireland, Austria and Finland -- for countries where progress towards convergence with Maastricht Treaty targets for entry to monetary union had been notable.
Portugal should be able to sustain its budget deficit at below three percent of gross domestic product (GDP), the target level for entry to EMU, in the years that followed, he said.
"We have sufficient room for manoeuvre on reducing the deficit as long as the political will is there," he said.
Bento said that inflation was probably the most difficult of the Maastricht criteria to meet for Portugal, but even this was attainable.

Ironically, the difficulty stemmed in part from Portugal's success in narrowing the gap between its standard of living -- so-called real convergence as opposed to nominal convergence -- and that of its richer European Union partners.
"Our success in the real convergence (brings) inevitably a rise in the relative price of non-tradable goods," he said.
Non-tradable goods include wages.
--Lisbon bureau 3511-3150035
